topic: How Does Your Heart Actually Work?
title: How Does Your Heart Actually Work? Inside Your Body's Nonstop Pump
hook: Right now, without you thinking about it, a muscle in your chest is squeezing, relaxing and squeezing again. It never takes a break. So what is it actually doing in there?
cta: Subscribe for more amazing body science!

beats.narration: Right now, without you thinking about it, a muscle in your chest is squeezing, relaxing and squeezing again. It never takes a break. So what is it actually doing in there?
You've felt it after running up the stairs, or in a scary movie, that thump, thump, thump getting faster. But most of us have no idea what's happening with each beat.
Here's what makes it mysterious. Your heart decides when to beat all by itself. No thought, no instruction from you. So who, or what, is giving the orders?

visual.title: Who tells your heart to beat?

beats.narration: An adult heart weighs only about 250 to 350 grams. Yet it moves blood through your entire body, every moment of your life.
Let's look inside. Your heart is split into a right side and a left side, and each side has two rooms, called chambers. That's four chambers in total.
The two top chambers are the atria. They're the receiving rooms, collecting blood as it returns. The two bottom chambers are the ventricles, the powerful pumping rooms that push blood out.
Big blood vessels connect at the top: the venae cavae bringing blood in, the pulmonary trunk heading to the lungs, and the aorta, the main highway out to your body.
But why would one heart need two separate sides? The answer is one of the cleverest designs in your body.
Your heart is really two pumps working side by side. The right side sends blood on a short loop to your lungs. The left side sends it on a long loop to the rest of your body.
Blood coming back from your body is low on oxygen. The right side pumps it into the lungs, where it picks up fresh oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide.
That oxygen-rich blood flows back into the left side. And the left side pumps it out through the aorta to your brain, your muscles, and every other part of you.
Think of it like a delivery service with two routes. One quick trip to the lungs to load up oxygen, then a long trip around the body to drop it off.
And in diagrams, oxygen-rich blood is usually drawn red and oxygen-poor blood blue. That's just a color code, so you can follow the two loops at a glance.
So what stops blood from sloshing backwards every time the heart squeezes?
Valves. Between the chambers, and at the exits, sit little flaps that act like one-way doors. In a healthy heart, they make sure blood only ever flows forward.
On the right side, the tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and the right ventricle. Each valve opens to let blood through, then closes behind it.
Now back to our mystery. Who's giving the orders?
The rhythm comes from a small group of special pacemaker cells in a spot called the sinoatrial node. They fire an electrical signal that sets off every single heartbeat.
Here's the surprising part: these pacemaker cells make up only about 1 percent of the heart's cells. A tiny team, running the whole show, for your entire life.

number.label: of heart cells set the rhythm

beats.narration: The signal spreads through the heart's own wiring, the conduction system, telling the chambers when to squeeze, in just the right order.
And a healthy heart isn't a perfect metronome. Researchers describe its rhythm as both complex and stable, constantly adjusting to what your body needs.
At rest, an adult heart beats about 72 times a minute. At that pace, each complete beat, called the cardiac cycle, takes about 0.8 seconds.
Those 0.8 seconds split into two phases. About 0.3 seconds of squeezing, called systole, pushes blood out. About 0.5 seconds of relaxing, called diastole, lets the chambers refill.
And here's something unexpected. About 80 percent of the blood flows into the ventricles before the atria even squeeze. The atria's push just tops them up.
Even stranger, your heart feeds itself mostly while it relaxes. Blood flow to the heart muscle's own vessels happens mainly during diastole, not while it squeezes.
Then the ventricles relax, the valves between the chambers open again, and the cycle begins once more. Squeeze, relax, repeat.
When you run, your body needs more oxygen, so your heart beats faster. When you rest, it slows down again. It's constantly listening and adjusting.
The heart even sits inside its own protective sac, the pericardium, which holds a small amount of fluid around it.
Doctors who specialize in the heart are called cardiologists. And if anything about your own heart ever worries you, talking to a doctor is always the right move.
So, how does your heart actually work? It's two pumps in one. The right side sends blood to your lungs for oxygen, and the left side sends it around your body.
One-way valves keep it flowing forward, and a tiny group of pacemaker cells sparks every beat, about 72 times a minute, squeeze and relax.
So next time you feel that thump in your chest, remember the tiny spark and the perfectly timed squeeze behind it. Stay curious!
